lines: Ever wonder who decides what things cost? Here's the secret. Nobody does. Buyers and sellers do it together, without even talking.
Start with buyers. When something gets cheaper, more people want it. When it gets pricier, fewer do. That's the law of demand.
Now sellers. When prices go up, selling gets more worth it, so more people bring stuff to sell. That's the law of supply.
Picture your bike stall. Price your bikes at two hundred dollars, and you'll stand there all day with a full table. That's a surplus.
Price them at forty, and there's a crowd, they're gone in ten minutes, and half the crowd leaves with nothing. That's a shortage. You left money on the table.
Somewhere in between is the price where the number of bikes people want matches the number you have. Economists call it equilibrium.
And here's the thing. That price moves. When school starts and every student needs a bike, demand shifts out, and the right price goes up.
When a big store opens down the street selling new bikes, demand shifts in, and the right price drops. When parts get cheaper, sellers bring more bikes, and supply shifts out.
One trick that shows up on every exam: if the bike's own price changes, you slide along the curve. If anything else changes, the whole curve shifts.
This same tug of war sets the price of rent, of concert tickets, of stocks, even of your future salary. Learn to read it, and prices stop being random.
